title: Maceration Time Modulates the In Vitro Antibacterial Activity of Ethanolic Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale) Extracts Against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus Isolates from Clinical Bovine Mastitis, with GC–MS Profiling of the Most Active Extract
content: Bovine mastitis caused by Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus remains a major driver of antimicrobial use in dairy herds, and the evaluation of plant extracts as possible complementary agents is hampered by poorly standardised extraction protocols that make published results difficult to compare. This preliminary in vitro study examined whether maceration time, a process variable rarely controlled in studies of Taraxacum officinale, modifies the antibacterial activity of ethanolic extracts against clinical mastitis isolates. Leaves and flowers were macerated in 96% ethanol for 1, 2, 4 and 6 days under otherwise constant conditions, and the extracts were screened by disc diffusion against one E. coli and one S. aureus isolate in a randomised complete block design (nine treatments, six replicate discs each, n = 54). Net inhibition diameter differed markedly among treatments (F = 262.43; p < 0.0001), and maceration time, microorganism and their interaction were significant in the block-adjusted factorial model (p < 0.0001). Extracts macerated for 1 to 4 days produced net zones of 1.33 to 5.67 mm, whereas the six-day extract produced 20.50 mm against E. coli and 9.50 mm against S. aureus. Because all extracts shared the same solvent, volume and application procedure, the time-dependent increase indicates that the activity of the six-day extract cannot be explained by the ethanol vehicle alone. GC–MS tentatively assigned 21 constituents in the six-day extract, dominated by linolenic acid (37.46%), linoleic acid (10.61%), palmitic acid (9.26%) and ethyl palmitate (8.94%). The novelty of the work lies in showing, within a single constant protocol, that extraction time alone can shift a dandelion extract from negligible to substantial in vitro activity, which identifies maceration time as an uncontrolled source of heterogeneity among published studies. These results establish the six-day macerate as the priority extract for quantitative evaluation by broth microdilution, bioguided fractionation and chemical comparison across maceration times.
